knowledge_point.title: Differentiating a Trigonometric Function Using the Chain Rule

question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $g(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(12-2x)$ and $h(x)=-6{x}^{3}.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =g(x)+h(x).\end{aligned}
$$

First, we differentiate $g(x).$ We express $g(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(12-2x)$ as the composite function

$$
g=\operatorname{cos}⁡u,\,u=12-2x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}u}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡u,\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-2.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡u\cdot (-2) \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡u \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(12-2x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate $h(x)=-6{x}^{3}.$ 

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}x}=-18{x}^{2}
$$

Hence,

$$
{f}^{′}(x)={g}^{′}(x)+{h}^{′}(x)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡(12-2x)-18{x}^{2}.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y=12\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-1)$ at the point $(1+\pi ,-12).$

{{selection}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, the slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=1+\pi $ is given by ${f}^{′}(1+\pi ).$

We will calculate ${f}^{′}(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
y=12\operatorname{cos}⁡u,\,u=x-1.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=-12\operatorname{sin}⁡u\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =-12\operatorname{sin}⁡u\cdot 1 \\  & =-12\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=1+\pi ,$ we find

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}m={f}^{′}(1+\pi ) & =-12\operatorname{sin}⁡(1+\pi -1) \\  & =-12\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi ) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we find the equation of the tangent at the point $(1+\pi ,-12):$

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-(-12) & =0(x-(1+\pi )) \\ y+12 & =0 \\ y & =-12.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Differentiating a Trigonometric Function Using the Chain Rule

question.:question/worked-solution:
The slope of $y = f(x)$ at $x=1$ is given by $f'(1).$

We will calculate $f'(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

\[
y = \sin{u}, \qquad u = \pi \left(8x^{2} +2x - 2\right).
\]

Differentiating gives
\[
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} = \cos{u}, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = \pi (16x + 2).
\]

We now apply the chain rule, and get

\begin{align*}
f'(x) &= \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}\\[5pt]

&=\cos u \cdot \pi (16x+2)\\[5pt]

&=\pi (16x+2)\cos u\\[5pt]

&=\pi (16x+2)\cos \left(  \pi \left(8x^{2} +2x - 2\right) \right).
\end{align*}

Evaluating at $x=1,$ we find

\begin{align}
f'(1) & =\pi (16\cdot1+2)\cos \left(  \pi \left(8\cdot1^{2} +2\cdot1 - 2\right) \right) \\[3pt]

& =18\pi \cos(8\pi) \\[3pt]
&= 18\pi \cdot (1) \\[3pt]
&= 18 \pi
\end{align}

Therefore, the slope $m$ of $y = f(x)$ at $x = 1$ is 
\[
m = f'(1) = \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{18 \pi}.
\]
